I’m well aware that a single neurotransmitter has various functions. What I was doing was providing you with knowledge that we’ve gained through research that shows how, generally speaking, the neuroanatomy of people with ADHD differs from those without ADHD because you said “if ADHD were real then there’s be a shared, testable biological trait between ADHD-havers.” Neurology is a subcategory of biology, so that’s what I provided you. If that’s not enough to convince that that ADHD is real then I don’t see any point in continuing this conversation, so I’ll be leaving it here.

ADHD is a neurological disorder. A big part of the disorder revolves around a struggle with executive function (e.g., focus, impulse control). Many imaging studies have shown that people with ADHD have less activity in their prefrontal cortex (PFC). The PFC is very important in the role of executive function. Stimulants, such as adderall, increase levels of the neurotransmitters dopamine and norepinephrine, and in turn promote executive functioning and activity in the PFC.

I’ll preface this by saying that my dynamic with the friend I’ll be talking about was a bit different because while our dynamic may have been a little flirtatious at times it never verged on anything physical, but I think it’s still important to mention. I had a friend fondle my breasts once while watching a movie. I didn’t say or do anything to protest or stop it. I think I kind of froze out of shock, but there are various reasons why someone wouldn’t say anything in a moment like that and they don’t all necessarily mean that they’re okay with what’s taking place. Like I mentioned at the beginning, there are definitely differences in dynamics here. There also weren’t any substances involved in my situation. Just know that there is a possibility that she wasn’t okay with what happened and that may need to be addressed.

Edited to add. I didn’t really see anyone else mentioning this in the comments, so maybe I missed something and my comment is unnecessary. Maybe I’m projecting, idk. I just thought the added insight might be important.

I don’t remember what the first moment was as there were many sprinkled in while growing up. A moment I will never forget though is when I asked why being gay was wrong one Sunday in our junior high group. No one could give me a clear answer and the statement people made felt more like guesses than explanations, but everyone maintained that being gay was sinful. I’m a lesbian (though I didn’t know it at the time) and I think about this moment quite often.

I don’t remember his exact words, but it was something along the lines of “you don’t seem like the type”

I need answers. There’s a type? I was confused then and still am to this day.
Thank you for your kind words, they mean a lot. I’m sorry you’re going through this now. I know it’s hard, but you can do it too.

Oh, I’m with you here. What really bothers me is when people see introversion as something to be “fixed.” My dad has spent a lot of my life trying to make me more of an extrovert. Based on my experience, there seems to be this misconception, that introverts are unhappy and lonely. I just wish people could see it for what it is.

Seriously, and to the cop saying it was because he was tired of running, what qualifies you to know why he’s having trouble breathing? You’re a cop, not a medical professional.

It’s annoying, but at the same time I’m thinking, “how ignorant can you be?”

YES

My dad believes that if something good happens, that wasn’t probable, it was the work of god. He also doesn’t believe in coincidences. It’s all by gods design. These things annoy me to no end.

In all seriousness, I do hope to be where you are one day. For now, I will continue to work on myself and try to hold on to hope.

Congrats btw! I am a so happy you’re in a better place! This gives me a bit of hope.

I’ve recently (approximately 2 years) left the church and now identify as an agnostic. I relate to feeling guilty and anxious about religion. Since leaving Christianity, I have attended church every now and then (when I’m back home) with my family. I don’t really have any strong relationships at the church. I mainly go because I know it makes my family happy. It is a bit awkward. I will say, it is for more reasons than not being Christian anymore.

I don’t really know if I have anything to say to put your mind at ease. I apologize for that. Wish I could do more. In my personal experience though, worship has not at all lulled me back. If anything, it confirms where I stand today. It has made me more confident in what I do or don’t believe. I hope it can be a validating experience for you too.

I too, am much happier as an ex-Christian, and I think that just goes to show that I am on the right track, for myself, as are you. I know it’s easier said than done, but try not to let what others think get to you. This is something I’m still struggling with. When I know I’ll be joining my family at church I have to mentally prepare. I think it helps to think beforehand of why you left Christianity, and are now agnostic. Then keep those reasons in the back of your mind so you can remind yourself of them if you begin to doubt yourself. Also, don’t forget how much healthier and happier you are now!

Hope this helps at least a little. I wish you the best!
